AJK.name: Juneau
AJK.excerpt: A secondary front will push northward in the S Panhandle through early Wednesday morning, bringing another round rain to the panhandle and elevated wind gusts up to 35 mph across Annette Island and S Prince of Wales Island into Wednesday afternoon.

sections.name: Long Term, Aviation, And Evening Forecast Update
paragraphs: Front continues to march northward across the panhandle, bringing widespread rain across much of the panhandle, with snow ongoing near Haines and along the Haines Highway. Minor update to the Winter Weather Advisory was the "expansion" to include the rest of Haines Borough and the Chilkat Peninsula, however no adjustments to amounts, up to 5 inches. Satellite derived snowfall rates indicated decent rates moving over the Haines/Chilkat area earlier with FAA web cams and local observations reporting visibilities sustained 1 mile or less, with imagery indicating another round of snow moving up Lynn Canal now.

A secondary front will push northward in the S Panhandle through early Wednesday morning, bringing another round rain to the panhandle and elevated wind gusts up to 35 mph across Annette Island and S Prince of Wales Island into Wednesday afternoon.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: You heard it here first folks. Sunday looks like a pretty nice day across much of the Panhandle and coast. Expect winds to start dying off Friday as our parade of lows comes to an end, allowing high pressure to once again briefly dominate, increasing the odds for a little sun, primarily Sunday. The biggest question in the extended forecast is a shortwave trough moving in from the western Gulf Saturday, which has a decent signal of colder air associated with it. 850mb temperatures near -5C certainly make one ponder the rain/snow line for Icy Strait; however, the long transit over relatively warm ocean waters will help warm the surface airmass, along with onshore southerly flow scrubbing out colder air at the surface, likely limiting sea level impacts to rain. Something to track through the rest of this week if this system starts trending colder, which could mean a hit of snow for Icy Strait north. Either way on Sunday, mariners looking to make moves across the inner channels should enjoy lighter winds, keeping a close eye on major inlets like Taiya, Taku, and Stikine for breezy northerly to easterly winds. This may help prime some northern communities for additional snow later on next week.

For folks operating along the mighty Gulf coast, fresh seas will wind down Friday with long period southerly swell flourishing, becoming westerly by the end of the weekend. By and large significant wave heights should reach near or below 5 to 7 ft by Sunday, existing within a more comfortable long period swell spectrum. The exception may be waters west of Prince of Wales where we could see 7 to 9 ft fresh seas from higher northwesterly winds. Monday, the Aleutian Storm Track opens up opportunities for storm development into the Gulf into next week.

High confidence for lighter winds in the inner channels and the overall marine forecast thru Sunday. Keep an eye for fog in the forecast as we move closer to the weekend. The largest uncertainty in the long range is cold air advection on the backside of the shortwave trough Saturday which has implications on precipitation type for the north. As of Tuesday night, the published forecast reflects high confidence for rain Saturday with room to pivot if the system trends colder.

sections.name: Prev Discussion
paragraphs: ...ISSUED AT 403 PM AKST Tue Nov 24 2026...
- A front continues to move north across the panhandle this evening bringing more rain and wind with snow expected for the northern panhandle.
- Multiple rounds of rain and wind are likely this week with the possibility of some drier and cooler weather this weekend.

SHORT TERM.../Through Thursday/...A front currently located over the central panhandle this afternoon will continue to push northwestward into tonight. This rather fast-moving front will bring more warm moist air into the panhandle, with quite a bit more moisture behind it and holding together more as it moves north compared to the front that passed through Monday night. This generally stronger front will bring rain across much of the area, with some snow mixing in around Gustavus over to Juneau but little to no accumulation expected before they see a transition to rain with the warmer temperatures and rising snow levels. Further north, including Skagway and Haines, will see snow at sea level again as it moves in this evening. With the orientation of the front and prevalent moisture with it, Haines and Skagway are expected to see snow accumulations of 0.5 to 1.5 inches by early Wednesday morning. Higher amounts are expected in higher elevations of the highways, with 1 to 3 inches along the Klondike Highway, and 2 to 5 inches along the Haines Highway by tomorrow morning. A Winter Weather Advisory has been issued for the Haines Highway past Milepost 24, as the higher elevations along the highway up to the border are expected to see 3 to 5 inches of new snow accumulation in the next 12 hours.

This system continues to also bring elevated winds to the area, particularly along the coast with the easterly winds as the front moves through and the low travels along the outer coast, and near Skagway with the northerly offshore flow as the low moves northward. Winds inland will begin to diminish into tonight as the low weakens and after the front passes.

Active weather continues into Wednesday and Thursday as another wave pushes through tonight into the day Wednesday behind this front, bringing more rain and warm air into the area. This next feature appears to begin to shear apart and pull westward after it reaches the Icy Strait area as another low approaches from the Pacific Wednesday, which looks to cut off some of the moisture of the feature ahead of it, as its associated front begins to push into the panhandle from the south Wednesday night. Overall rain is expected for much of the panhandle as these multiple systems keep an inflow of warm, moist air into the panhandle, however the continued northerly flow over the northern panhandle will help keep colder air in place for longer even as the rest of the panhandle sees a warming trend. Skagway and Haines will continue to see snow, though uncertainty will remain on how far the systems progress northward and with how much moisture that will affect any further snow accumulations. Gustavus, Juneau, and Yakutat may also see some potential for mixed precipitation if the gaps between systems allow for the areas to cool enough, but generally with each system will be lower snow potential than the last.

Multiple systems working their way over the panhandle through the week today, with the first stronger system currently near Fredrick Sound at time of writing. The second, weaker front, moves up from the south overnight tonight into Wednesday morning, and the third, slightly stronger gale force system, moves up from the south early Thursday morning

Strong gale force winds will decay to gale force winds as the low pressure system and associated front reaches the waters outside Cross Sound. Near Cross Sound, the front will get a slight boost from a tip jet from southeasterlies and easterlies out of Cross Sound. Wave Heights, capping around 20 ft, will subside through the night to 11-14 ft across the gulf, with winds between 20-25 knots. The third, stronger low moves into the southern panhandle Wednesday night into Thursday. Confidence is moderate to low for this system's track and strength, and could see another round of gales for western coast of Prince of Wales Island.

For changes to the ongoing forecast, not many are present, with the main changes being the gale warning issued for Clarence Strait for this frontal passage, along with the extension of the higher winds for Lynn Canal. Point Couverden continues to overperform due to a persistent tip jet, with gale force winds and near storm force gusts. As the front moves northward, expect to see a transition from northerly to southeasterly for the Icy Strait corridor, Stephens Passage, and northern Chatham Strait (specifically Peril Strait).

The third low pressure system moving into the southern panhandle on Wednesday could bring another round of gales for Clarence, though as mentioned before, confidence is lower for the strength and track of this system.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: High pressure will build into the region on Sunday, bringing a brief respite from the wet holiday week. This looks to be short- lived, as another shortwave trough moves into the region on Monday and Tuesday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light valley rain and mountain snow in eastern Oregon into central Idaho tapering off by the mid afternoon.
- Widespread precipitation and above normal temperatures on Thanksgiving Day through early Saturday. Gusty winds will occur across southern areas late Friday.
- High snow levels above 7000 feet MSL by Friday will shift most precipitation over the region.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A weak warm front will move through southeast Oregon this morning. Widespread cloud cover and elevated east/southeast winds are keeping temperatures warm this evening, with Baker City and Burns both above freezing as of 2am. A pocket of clearing in central Oregon could allow temperatures to drop below freezing before sunrise. Warm air and precipitation will move over these colder pockets, bringing a 10% chance of freezing rain to Burns this morning. Baker City and the I-84 corridor will see rain as the predominant precipitation type. Snow levels will hover around 4500-5500 ft MSL through the morning, with hi-res models showing a few pockets of heavier precipitation at times through the morning. Valley rain showers and mountain snow showers will move into the Treasure Valley and the Central ID Mountains by mid-morning. Snow amounts will generally be light with less than an inch of accumulation today, but localized higher amounts are possible in those heavier showers. Widespread warming and drying will occur by the early evening, with overnight clearing early allowing for fog formation in high terrain valleys.

A robust atmospheric river will then move onshore by Thanksgiving Day, with a band of heavy rain and high elevation mountain snow moving in from the northwest by the afternoon. Cold pools lingering in mountain valleys, primarily in northeast Oregon, will again present a threat for freezing rain. This could create difficult travel conditions on the I-84 corridor in Baker County and just northwest of Ontario, OR. Strong zonal flow aloft will allow for high winds aloft, so forecast reflects the potential shadowing and lower precipitation chances, especially in the Baker Valley and the Treasure Valley. This moisture plume will continue through the end of the short term, steadily increasing the precipitation chances southward each day. The Magic Valley will finally see precipitation by Friday evening. Warm air moving in from the south and west will elevate snow levels to 7500-8500 ft MSL by Friday, with most populated areas in the mountains seeing rain on Friday. Snow levels might be slightly lower around 6000-7000 ft MSL in northern Adams/Valley County. Total accumulations for higher elevation snow from Thursday to Saturday will range from 6-12 inches above about 7000 feet in the Central ID Mountains and Wallowa Mountains. Gusty winds will also peak on Friday and Saturday on mountain summits and in high terrain southwest of the Snake River Valley with gusts up to 35-45 mph by Friday evening. Temperatures will be about 5-10 degrees above normal through the short term period.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: High pressure will build into the region on Sunday, bringing a brief respite from the wet holiday week. This looks to be short- lived, as another shortwave trough moves into the region on Monday and Tuesday. This will bring slightly cooler temperatures, lower snow levels back down to 5000-6000 ft MSL, and another push of valley rain and mountain snow. Ridging will attempt to build back in on Wednesday, but a closed low just off the coast of California will move through the region, splitting the upper level flow and bringing cooler air and precipitation to the southern tier of the region. Model uncertainty remains on the timing and positioning of the low, but most solutions and ensemble members agree that the bulk of the precipitation will be to our south over the Desert Southwest. Current forecast keeps a 20-40% chance of precipitation over the region through Wednesday, with temperatures lingering slightly above normal. Interestingly enough, the potential for a hard freeze in the Boise metro area appears to still not occur by early December. This would be the latest freeze on record, with the previous latest freeze occurring November 16th, 2016.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Temperatures will drop closer to normal for the weekend, with highs in the 40s and low 50s. Forecast uncertainty continues for early next week as models show very different solutions on the potential progression of another shortwave and front Monday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A gradual warming trend likely through the rest of the workweek, with quiet weather expected through Thanksgiving.
- Gusty winds expected along the northern Front Range on Friday and Saturday.
- Next storm system could bring snow to the mountains this weekend, with lower confidence for precipitation over the plains.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Above-normal temperatures and dry conditions will prevail through much of the work week. Weak upper level ridging will be near the area as a strong upper low sits to our east and a trough moves onto the West Coast Wednesday. For Thanksgiving, temperatures will be in the upper 40s to mid 50s for the plains and the 30s and 40s for the higher terrain. Winds will be on the lighter side for the plains (generally less than 15mph) with mostly sunny skies on Thursday. Temperatures will peak on Friday with highs in the low 60s for much of the plains.

On Friday, an upper level low is forecast to develop to our north/northeast over Canada and a strong high is forecast to develop to our southwest over the Pacific. This will put us in an area of strong northwest winds aloft. Winds will start to pick up in the higher terrain overnight Thursday into Friday, peaking Saturday morning. Stronger winds could make it onto the plains on Saturday as a cold front is dragged through the area. However, there is still a lot of model uncertainty with the system this weekend. The ECMWF is still showing a more potent shortwave moving through on Saturday with a strong cold front. While the GFS has a much more subtle shortwave and weaker front. Other models are more on board with the Euro than the GFS. Also, the GFS is trending slightly stronger with the front in latest runs. This has us leaning more towards the stronger front and better precip chances solution fort his weekend. Confidence is high in snow falling in our northern mountains, with decreasing confidence as we go further south and further east on the plains. Chances for snow on the plains will depend on the shortwave and timing/strength of the front, with the current NBM at a low to medium chance (10% to 40%) for at least a trace of snow across the plains by Sunday morning.

Temperatures will drop closer to normal for the weekend, with highs in the 40s and low 50s. Forecast uncertainty continues for early next week as models show very different solutions on the potential progression of another shortwave and front Monday.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Moving into Sunday and the start of next week we should briefly dry out with cooler temperatures on tap, warming back into Monday as another shortwave passes across the region.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - High winds are possible Thursday night through Saturday night. A High Wind Watch is currently in effect for the southeast Wyoming wind prone areas.
- Forecast uncertainty in regards to precipitation remains high over the weekend due to notable model variance.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Looking at a quiet weather day for the forecast area on Wednesday. Upper-level ridging will move into the Rockies, keeping temperatures similar to what they were on Tuesday. Subsidence under the ridge will keep precipitation chances away, as well as cloud cover for much of the day. Winds under the ridge will also be weak, leading to an uneventful day. Anyone traveling across southeast Wyoming or western Nebraska for Thanksgiving today will encounter great weather. Clouds will begin to increase later in the afternoon and overnight ahead of a weak shortwave moving into the area. Conditions overnight will be equally calm, with low temperatures roughly average for this time of year.

Expect mostly similar weather for Thanksgiving day. The forecast area will still be under the influence of the ridge, so dry conditions will prevail with mostly sunny skies. Temperatures will actually be warmer compared to Wednesday, with the warmest highs along the Interstate 25 corridor. High temperatures in the 40s and 50s are expected, which is anywhere from 5 to 10 degrees above average for late November. The biggest difference from Wednesday, is that Thursday will see increasing winds, especially in southeast Wyoming from the weak shortwave that will move across the CWA. The strongest winds are expected Thursday night as MSLP gradients steepen. CAG to CPR height gradients will also show a response, climbing into the 50 to 60 meter range. Winds aloft overnight will reach about 55 to 60 kts with decent subsidence. As a result, high winds will be possible in the typical wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming, including Arlington, Bordeaux, and the South Laramie Range and foothills. A High Wind Watch has been issued for these areas beginning Thursday evening. Wind gusts of 55 to 65 MPH will be possible, with localized gusts to 70 MPH.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Continued uncertainty expected in the long term forecast due to model variance with differing amounts of precipitation possible, but no matter what a system will move through the region and bring strong winds with temperatures likely dropping as this moves through the region. Thursday into Friday the upper level transient ridge will continue it's progression through the region as it makes way for a strong Pacific trough and jet that will start to overtake by the end of the week. At the surface we'll see another dry and warm day for the Thanksgiving holiday with incoming cloudiness in response to the approaching system. On Friday upslope flow across the mountains increases, allowing wintry precipitation to resume for them. Winds meanwhile will ramp up late Thursday into Friday, and continue through Saturday before finally lessening, likely bringing a multi-day high wind event for our wind prone locations. Most guidance is in solid agreement on this already, with in-house models showing a 40-60% probability of high winds for the wind prones, and 850 mb pressure gradients of 60 to 80 meters, giving high confidence to the likelihood of this event.

What's less likely is precipitation outside of the mountains, with a wide swath of outcomes from all ensemble members. Everything from our usual dry conditions to Cheyenne seeing near 6 inches of snowfall is on the table. The higher precipitation chance scenarios also bring with them cooler temperatures, while the drier scenarios from the system just a bit further east bring warmer temperatures. As of this writing I would say ensembles seem to be favoring the lower elevations finally getting at least some meager precipitation, so hopefully Cheyenne will finally see it's first noteworthy accumulating snowfall this record setting year, but to what amount is still up in the air.

Moving into Sunday and the start of next week we should briefly dry out with cooler temperatures on tap, warming back into Monday as another shortwave passes across the region. This one will yet again feature the strongest forcing well to our south, so expect any precipitation to be limited once again to the mountains from orographic enhancement. Overall an active end to November, and hopefully we can finally achieve some precipitation for our incredibly dry eastern zones.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: On Friday and into Saturday, the ridge over Southern California breaks down which will bring northwesterly flow. Confidence is high on a system moving through within this time frame but there are varying solutions and impacts.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mild and dry conditions expected through Thanksgiving.
- Patchy fog is possible in lower valleys Wednesday morning especially in southern Colorado.

- There is increasing confidence in active weather for the holiday weekend, but exact details remain uncertain at this time. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available especially if traveling.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: MILD AND DRY CONDITIONS THROUGH THANKSGIVING:

A fast moving ridge continues to build over our area. Wednesday will look similar to today with generally mild and dry conditions expected. Patchy fog may develop again Wednesday morning in the lower valleys due to clear skies, light winds, and high relative humidity from our recent system. Highest confidence would be in southern Colorado with potential for fog formation in the Uinta Basin. The ridge shifts eastward Wednesday night into Thursday. As this occurs, a new ridge will build over Southern California and create a split flow pattern for Thanksgiving. This leads to our region being sandwiched between a cutoff low to our south while another powerful system develops to our north and east. A continuation of dry conditions with above-normal temperatures is expected for Thanksgiving as both systems move away from our CWA.
ANOTHER SYSTEM EXPECTED AFTER THANKSGIVING:

On Friday and into Saturday, the ridge over Southern California breaks down which will bring northwesterly flow. Confidence is high on a system moving through within this time frame but there are varying solutions and impacts. The GFS is showing a 250mb jet max setting up over Wyoming and a weaker shortwave with lesser snowfall totals primarily confined to the Park Range. The Euro is showing a stronger jet max setting up further south over western Colorado and eastern Utah with a more amplified, stronger trough. This stronger scenario would lead to higher snowfall totals with impacts potentially extending as far south as the I-70 corridor. Due to these differing scenarios, confidence in impacts and exact amounts remains low. Confidence is highest over the Park Range with lowering confidence to the south. Anyone traveling late this week and this weekend should prepare for potentially difficult conditions. Looking ahead, there are some indications of another system impacting the region early next week but guidance diverges on specific scenarios.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Monday to Wednesday...models begin to diverge for early to mid next week. Overall, it looks dry, with showers possible mainly along the Continental Divide.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and mild with temperatures in the 50s to 60s through Friday.
- A quick moving storm system will bring wind to the Plains and snow showers to the Central Mountains on Saturday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...broad northwesterly flow aloft continues across Colorado as high pressure build across Utah. This has led to passing mid and high clouds across the region early this morning. Temperatures are currently in the 20s across the Plains, with a few more degrees of cooling expected through sunrise.

Today and tonight...upper level high pressure shift eastward out of Utah and across Colorado through tonight. This will lead to quiet weather across the region. Temperatures will warm into the upper 40s to lower 50s for highs this afternoon. Overnight lows will fall into the teens and 20s by Thursday morning.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: There is better agreement through the weekend with regards to a passing upper trough, with larger differences by early next week.

Thursday and Friday...overall, quiet weather will continue through the end of the work week across southern Colorado. Thursday look nice across the region, with upper 40s to mid 50s for highs across the Plains. Overnight lows will fall into the 20s and 30s across the Plains and teens for the San Luis Valley.

On Friday, northwesterly flow increases across the region. Enhanced mixing will help temperatures warm nicely into the upper 50s to mid 60s on the Plains, with a few areas pushing 70 degrees. Winds will also be increasing, especially in gap wind and wind prone areas along the lee slopes of the Eastern Mountains. Gusts of 30 to 35 mph are possible in these areas. This will also help keep overnight temperatures warm with mostly 30s across the Plains, and 20s for the San Luis Valley.

Saturday into Sunday...models are in better agreement with a quick moving upper wave moving in the northwesterly flow across Colorado. The GFS remain less aggressive than the ECMWF, but the ECMWF is less amplified than it was yesterday. Saturday looks windy with the upper trough passage. Northwest winds with gusts 40 to 50 mph are possible across the Plains. Humidity values look to remain elevated, limiting any fire weather concerns. Showers will also develop across the Central Mountains on Saturday and continue into the evening hours. Current QPF amounts are low, and snow amounts of less than an inch are possible for areas north of Cottonwood Pass. The ECMWF is still a bit more amplified with the system, and spreads showers off the higher terrain into the Pikes Peak Region Saturday evening. NBM guidance is in the middle, with low pops across the Palmer Divide. At this time, the remainder of the area looks to remain dry. Slightly cooler temperatures are forecast for Saturday, with 50s and lower 60s across the region.

The upper wave quickly shift eastward by Sunday, with a return to dry conditions. Winds will also weaken, and temperatures will be cooler after the trough passage. Highs will only reach into the 40s for much of the Plains.

Monday to Wednesday...models begin to diverge for early to mid next week. Overall, it looks dry, with showers possible mainly along the Continental Divide. There is some potential for the next storm system by Wednesday, but timing is really up in the air at this time. Temperatures look to remain mild with 50s across the region.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Confidence remains fairly high in a transition to a more progressive and active pattern next week, as a series of shortwave troughs move inland and pass through the region.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - High pressure will bring dry weather and near-seasonal temperatures across the area through Thanksgiving.
- A more mild airmass will spread across the region for the upcoming weekend, boosting temperatures 5 to 10 degrees above normal for late November.
- A weather system brushing by northern Utah Friday night through early Saturday will bring a chance of valley rain and mountain snow mainly north of I-80.

- A more active weather pattern will return next week as a series of weather systems pass through the region. This far out, considerable uncertainty remains regarding the timing and track of these systems.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Mid level ridging centered across the forecast area is maintaining dry and stable conditions this evening. Warming aloft is resulting in an inversion layer a couple thousand feet above the northern valley floors, which is limiting ventilation and reducing air quality into the moderate category presently. A mean ridge will remain across the region through Thanksgiving, maintaining dry and stable conditions with inversions persisting across northern valleys and basins. This may allow for patchy late night/early morning fog in sheltered locations such as the Cache Valley and near the GSL. A weak shortwave fighting through this ridge will split as it moves through the Great Basin, having little if any discernible impact on the forecast area. With this ridge remaining in place, a gradual warming trend is expected across central and southern Utah through the remainder of the week.

A shortwave trough brushing by to the northeast is forecast to push a cold front through the area Friday night into Saturday. EC ensemble members remain more aggressive digging this wave a little further west, and bringing a round of valley rain/mountain snow to northern and perhaps portions of central Utah Friday night into early Saturday. GEFS members continue to remain drier so some uncertainty does remain.

Confidence remains fairly high in a transition to a more progressive and active pattern next week, as a series of shortwave troughs move inland and pass through the region. Uncertainty remains regarding timing and track of these waves and the resultant chances for precipitation, however late Tuesday into Wednesday looks most likely for widespread precipitation across the forecast area.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: You can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you on slopes steeper than about 30 degrees at higher elevations. The most dangerous slopes are those with wind-drifted snow that face west to north through east. If you experience audible collapsing or shooting cracks, give suspect slopes a wide buffer and stick to lower-angle terrain, as you can trigger avalanches from a distance or from below.
Slopes less than 30 degrees in wind-sheltered areas and slopes below treeline offer safer travel options.

2753.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Stiffer wind-drifted slopes on steep northwest to north to east-facing aspects are still dangerous and should be avoided. You can find these in isolated pockets in thinner areas, or they can be well connected in deeper snowpacks and triggered from a distance. By sticking to lower-angle, sheltered slopes, or more southerly aspects, you will lessen your odds of triggering a slide.

2754.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe from avalanches due to thin and discontinuous snow cover. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche where recent winds have formed isolated pockets of stiff snow below ridgelines, on lee slopes, and around rocky outcrops in the alpine.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe to travel on as there is very little snow. In the alpine, steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetops.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

1736.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Elevations above 7,000 feet have 1-2 feet of snow on the ground. You may encounter pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north- and east-facing terrain. If the snow feels stiff or slabby underfoot, then find a different aspect away from wind-drifted snow. The biggest hazard remains thin snow cover and hitting rocks, logs, and stumps. Even a small slide through thin coverage could end a season before it even starts.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: Above 7,000 feet, a layered snowpack is beginning to build for the season. Good, albeit thin, skiing and riding conditions have been reported at upper elevations. Elevations below 7,000 feet remain thin and bony. Before November 13th, most slopes were bare. Winter trailhead access remains a challenge as there is not quite enough snow to launch sleds. Most forest roads become impassable by vehicle above 6,500 feet. As folks start poking around the mountains, remember that avalanches can occur with just a few feet of snow on the ground. There may be some lingering pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north and east-facing terrain features, particularly just below ridgelines.

Beginning Thanksgiving Day, a large storm system will impact the Pacific and Interior Northwest. Strong winds, mountain snow, and fluctuating rain/snow levels will be in the cards for several days. Pay attention to changing weather and snow conditions heading into the weekend. Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

Fresh wind slabs will come back onto the menu with more snow and wind later this week. Pay attention to gullies that can become crossloaded and may also act as a terrain trap. Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices. Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
Turn On Your Snow and Avalanche Brain

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).

• Help us paint a picture of what's going on in the mountains. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps forecasters and the public alike.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: In very isolated spots, you may find a drift of firm snow resting on old, weak snow. In steep terrain, steer clear of these areas to reduce avalanche risk. Unfortunately, these will also be the most attractive areas to ride.
